quiz.q: What does `std::env::var("KEY")` return when KEY isn't set?
quiz.explain: env::var returns Result<String, VarError>. A missing variable is an Err, never a silent empty string — Rust won't let 'missing' and 'set to empty' look the same.

quiz.q: Why shouldn't real secrets live in a committed `.env` file?
options: Rust refuses to compile projects with .env files
.env files only work in test builds
Once a secret is in git history, it's compromised — rotating it is the only real fix
dotenvy encrypts the file automatically, so it's fine either way
quiz.explain: A committed .env eventually ends up in every clone and fork forever. Treat it as local-dev convenience only; real secrets belong in the platform's secret manager.

options: At the very end of main, after all env::var calls
Once, early in main, before you read anything with env::var
Inside every function that needs an env var
It's called automatically by Cargo before main runs
quiz.explain: It has to run before the reads that depend on it — calling it late means the vars it would have loaded aren't there yet.

quiz.q: Why deserialize config into a `#[derive(Deserialize)]` struct instead of many loose `env::var` calls?
options: It's the only way to read a file in Rust
Field types are checked, and a missing or wrong field gives one clear error instead of scattered bugs
It removes the need for a Cargo.toml file
env::var can't return numeric values at all
quiz.explain: Once you have more than a couple of related settings, a typed struct catches problems at startup with one clear message instead of tracking down a bug three functions later.

quiz.q: What's the problem with `env::var("KEY").unwrap_or_default()` for a setting that must be configured correctly?
options: It silently treats 'missing' the same as 'set to empty on purpose,' hiding real misconfiguration
quiz.explain: Falling back to a default on error can be fine for optional settings, but it can also mask a real problem — a required var that's simply not set.

quiz.q: Which crate does this lesson use to load a `.env` file into the process environment?
quiz.explain: dotenvy::dotenv() reads a .env file and copies its key-value pairs into the process environment, so env::var finds them normally afterward.

quiz.q: What should a committed `.env.example` file contain?
options: Nothing — it should be an empty file
The key names with fake/placeholder values, no real secrets
quiz.explain: .env.example documents which variables a project needs without leaking any actual secret values.

quiz.q: What is the return type of `env::var("KEY")`?
quiz.explain: It's a Result, not a String — reading the environment can fail (the variable might not exist), so the type says so.

flashcards.back: Result<String, VarError> — Ok(value) if set, Err if missing. Never a silent empty string.

flashcards.front: Where should real secrets live for production?
flashcards.back: In the platform's real secret manager — never in a committed .env file. .env is for local dev convenience only.
Once, at the very top of main, before any env::var reads that depend on it.

flashcards.front: What's the safer alternative to committing a real .env file?
flashcards.back: Add .env to .gitignore and commit a .env.example with key names but no real values.

flashcards.front: When should you switch from loose env::var calls to a config struct?
flashcards.back: Once you have more than a couple of related settings — deserialize a TOML/JSON file into a #[derive(Deserialize)] struct instead.

flashcards.front: Why prefer .expect("message") over bare .unwrap() on a required env var?
flashcards.back: .expect gives a clear, custom message about exactly what's missing; bare .unwrap() just says 'called unwrap on an Err value.'

flashcards.front: What crate/function deserializes a TOML file into a struct?
flashcards.back: toml::from_str, combined with #[derive(Deserialize)] from serde on the target struct.
